summary:
Consensual same-sex conduct is lawful in Mozambique. The colonial-era 'vices against nature' provision was erased in the 2015 revision of the penal code, and the code now in force, Law 24/2019 (effective 2020), carries no prohibition on consensual conduct. A trans visitor faces no criminal exposure on the basis of gender identity or consensual sexual conduct.

The penal code provides hate-crime and hate-speech protections that name gender identity. Article 191 prohibits incitement to discrimination, hatred or violence against a person or group on the basis of gender identity, and reaches defamation, insults and threats directed at transgender people. Article 160 makes a victim's sexual orientation or gender identity an aggravating factor in homicide. The Advertising Code (2016) bars advertisements containing discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation. These are the statutory protections a trans visitor could invoke.

No legal gender recognition procedure exists. There is no route under Mozambican law for a trans person to change the gender marker on identity documents. A visitor whose passport or other documents carry markers inconsistent with their presentation should expect that mismatch to be visible at checkpoints and in any interaction requiring identification. The sources describe no formal screening process for trans travellers and offer no assurance that none occurs.

Anti-discrimination law does not cover sexual orientation or gender identity in education, health, housing or employment. Employment protections that had been in place since 2007 were repealed by Labor Law No. 13/2023, effective February 2024. Discrimination on those grounds in education, health, housing or employment is not prohibited by law.

Violence against LGBTQ people is documented as rare, with discrimination the more common experience. Lambda Mozambique's Carina Capitine said the community is not targeted by violence as in some other African countries but does face discrimination.

Mozambique does not recognise same-sex relationships. Same-sex couples cannot marry or adopt. A trans visitor in a relationship that would be read locally as same-sex under birth-sex status has no route to legal recognition, and no spousal rights or protections follow from the relationship.
tangentialFactors:
Regional comparison: an Afrobarometer survey reported in 2016 found 56% of Mozambicans would welcome or not be bothered by a homosexual neighbour, against 5% in Uganda, Burkina Faso and Niger, placing Mozambique among the more tolerant jurisdictions in the region.

Public opinion polling is more permissive than the statute book. A 2017 ILGA poll found 61% of Mozambicans agreed that gay, lesbian and bisexual people should enjoy the same rights as straight people, and 55% believed transgender people should be allowed to change their legal gender. A 2017 survey found support for same-sex marriage at 47% in Maputo and between 38% and 42% in Beira and Nampula.

The 2015 penal code revision was the pivot for organised advocacy: Lambda Mozambique, then not yet registered, moved from decriminalisation campaigning to anti-discrimination lobbying.
localsOnly:
Lambda Mozambique, the country's only LGBT organisation, was blocked from registering as an NGO from 2008 onward, prompting a UN appeal in 2010. In October 2017 the Constitutional Council struck down the 'moral order' clause (Article 1 of Law No. 8/91) that had been used to refuse registration, ruling it unconstitutional; the council had earlier held that Lambda's status did not violate the constitution. Registration followed.

LGBTIQ residents face family ostracisation and barriers in employment and education. Most respondents to a 2017 survey said they would not accept a child who came out; 28% of Beira respondents said they would assault their child if he or she was gay. The same survey found 85% opposed violence against LGBTQ people and would help if they were being physically assaulted, and about one-third personally knew an openly LGBTQ person. A 2013 survey found moderate support for parenting rights.

Protests seeking same-sex marriage and common-law marriage recognition have run since 2006. A 2024 opposition pledge by PODEMOS raised community expectations on LGBTIQ issues and then disappointed them.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Human Rights Watch World Report 2024 chapter on Mozambique, published 11 January 2024, records general police detentions and election-related arrests. It carries no transgender-specific content and no information on where transgender prisoners are housed.

Enforcement of Article 191 and Article 160 is not documented in the sources. Whether prosecutions or civil claims under either provision have occurred is unresolved.

No formal screening process for trans travellers at Mozambican entry points or checkpoints is documented. The absence of a documented process is not evidence that none occurs, and no source addresses how officials handle document-marker mismatches in practice.
